idea:
Replace the random order with a target-likeness filter built on a bigram language model fitted to target_sample.

1. Tokenise target_sample and all docs with tiktoken gpt2 (encode_ordinary_batch; cap scoring at the first 2,000 tokens per doc for speed, but record full token counts).
2. Fit an add-k / interpolated bigram model on the target_sample tokens: p = 0.7 * bigram + 0.3 * unigram, with add-1 unigram smoothing. Hash the pair (a * 50257 + b) into numpy arrays or a dict.
3. Score each doc by mean per-token negative log-likelihood under this model. This penalises off-domain text (spam, code, Q&A) through the vocabulary, and word-shuffled Wikipedia articles through the bigram term, which a unigram or TF-IDF filter would miss.
4. Drop exact and near duplicates: keep the first occurrence by hash of the whitespace-normalised, lowercased first 500 characters. Also drop docs under 50 tokens.
5. Pick the threshold by 1-D 2-means (KMeans, k=2, seeded) on the scores and keep the low-NLL cluster. If the kept docs total less than 0.5 T tokens, widen to the best-scoring docs until 0.5 T is reached. If they total more than T, keep the best-scoring T tokens' worth.
6. Return the kept indices shuffled with CURATE_SEED. If under T tokens, let the trainer cycle the clean set rather than padding with junk.
why: The pool preview shows most documents are spam, code, Q&A or word-shuffled wiki articles, so spending all T tokens on deduplicated, well-ordered WikiText-like documents should cut bpb far more than any ordering change.
outcome: dev 1.9345 against 1.9411 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: Add a self-training second pass to the bigram filter. Keep the current pipeline as pass 1 (bigram model from target_sample, 2-means threshold). Then: (a) take the pass-1 low-NLL cluster as pseudo-target and refit the same interpolated bigram model (0.7 bigram + 0.3 add-1 unigram) on target_sample plus the first 2,000 tokens of every pass-1 kept doc. (b) Rescore every candidate with this larger model, leave-one-out: for a doc that was in the fit set, subtract its own bigram, context and unigram counts before computing its probabilities, so it cannot score itself well. (c) Score = mean per-token NLL over the first 2,000 tokens. Also compute the worst mean NLL over non-overlapping 256-token windows, and reject docs whose worst window is above the pass-2 2-means threshold by more than 1.0 nat, to catch partly damaged docs. (d) Re-run 1-D 2-means on the pass-2 scores and keep the low cluster, with the same 0.5 T floor and T cap, then the seeded shuffle. Also strengthen dedup: besides the first-500-chars hash, drop a doc if the hash of its tokens 100 to 300 (body, skipping the title line) was already seen, so duplicates with a perturbed title or opening are removed.
why: A bigram model fitted on only 200 target docs is too sparse to separate clean articles from word-shuffled or lightly corrupted ones, whereas refitting on the several million tokens of pass-1 pseudo-target text should give a much sharper bigram signal and a cleaner threshold, and the body-hash dedup should catch the near-duplicates that the title-based hash misses.
outcome: dev 1.9172 against 1.9345 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea:
Keep the current selection of the core set (dedup, two-pass bigram, worst-window rejection, 2-means low cluster, 0.5 T floor, T cap) unchanged, but change what happens when the core set has K < T tokens, and change the order.

1. If K < T, do not let the trainer cycle the core. Fill the missing T - K tokens with clean off-domain English "filler" docs instead. Filler candidates are deduplicated docs of at least 50 tokens that are not in the core, taken in ascending pass-2 mean NLL, and each must pass three junk guards:
(a) Scrambled text: at least 80% of its lowercased alphabetic words (first 2,000 characters) appear in a vocabulary built from target_sample plus the core docs.
(b) Template spam: len(zlib.compress(text)) / len(text) >= 0.35 on the first 4,000 characters, and the doc contains none of the 50 word 6-grams with the highest document frequency among non-core docs (count 6-grams over the first 300 words of each non-core doc; only 6-grams occurring in more than 1% of non-core docs count as banned).
(c) Pass-2 mean NLL below the midpoint between the 2-means high-cluster centre and the threshold; skip this guard if it leaves under 0.2 T tokens.
Stop adding filler once filler tokens reach T - K minus 20,000.

2. Order: filler first (seeded shuffle), then all core docs (seeded shuffle). The trainer then spends its last, low-learning-rate steps only on target-like text. After the core, append the 200 best-scoring core docs again as padding, so any overshoot or cycling past T lands on in-domain text rather than on filler.

3. If K >= T, output only the core, in seeded shuffle, as now.

Log K/T and the filler token count.
why: If the clean core is under T tokens, the trainer currently repeats it within a 300-step run, and fresh clean English placed early should teach more general language than those repeats while the in-domain text at the end keeps the final model fitted to the target style.
outcome: dev 1.9222 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Tighten the cleanliness of the core set in two ways, leaving the rest of the pipeline (two-pass bigram, 2-means, 0.5 T floor, T cap, seeded shuffle) unchanged.

**1. Full-length damage check.** Scoring currently sees only the first 2,000 tokens, so damage later in a long article is invisible.
- Keep the full token arrays. Passes 1 and 2 and their thresholds stay on the capped arrays, as now.
- After pass 2, take every candidate longer than 2,000 tokens with pass-2 mean NLL <= thr2 + 0.5.
- Score its full token array with model2, leave-one-out as now, in token-bounded chunks. Only the capped prefix was in the fit set, so subtract only the prefix counts; simplest is to compute own counts on the first 2,000 tokens and apply them to the whole doc, clipped at 0.
- Replace its worst-window value with the worst over all 256-token windows of the full doc.
- Add a second statistic: the fraction of 256-token windows with mean NLL > thr2 + 0.5. Reject a doc if its worst window > thr2 + 1.0 (as now) or if this fraction > 0.2.

**2. Position-invariant near-duplicate removal on the survivors.**
- For each surviving doc, compute hashes of all token 8-grams over the full doc with numpy. Use a polynomial hash in uint64: sum of tok[i+j] * P**j with wraparound.
- Keep only content-sampled shingles, those with hash % 8 == 0.
- Process docs in ascending pass-2 NLL. Drop a doc if it has at least 5 sampled shingles and at least 40% of them are already in the set of shingles from previously kept docs. Otherwise keep it and add its shingles to the set.
- This runs before the floor and cap logic, and the existing head and body hash dedup stays as a cheap prefilter.

Log the number of docs and tokens removed by each step and the final K/T.
why: Long articles damaged after token 2,000 and duplicates with shifted or perturbed text probably still get into the core, wasting the fixed token budget on noise and repeats, so removing them should lower held-out bpb.
outcome: dev 1.9546 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Keep the core selection exactly as now (dedup, two-pass bigram, 2-means, worst-window rejection, 0.5 T floor, T cap). Change only what happens when the core has K < T tokens: fill the gap with fresh, mostly-clean in-domain text instead of letting the trainer cycle the core.

1. Build a 'near-core' tier: deduplicated candidates of at least 50 tokens whose pass-2 mean NLL is in the low cluster (scores2 <= thr2) but which were rejected only by the worst-window test (worst2 > thr2 + 1.0). These are target-like articles with a locally damaged patch.
2. Sort near-core docs by ascending worst-window NLL (least damaged first). Add them until their tokens reach T - K, and never add a doc with worst2 > thr2 + 3.0.
3. Order: near-core docs first (seeded shuffle), then the core docs (seeded shuffle), so the late low-learning-rate steps see only clean core text.
4. If core plus near-core is still under T tokens, append a second, differently seeded shuffle of the core (seed + 1) until the list covers at least T tokens, so the trainer never wraps around to the near-core docs.
5. If K >= T, output is unchanged from the current best.

Log K/T, the number of near-core docs available, their token total, and the tokens actually added.
why: Experiment 4's large loss from shrinking the core suggests unique in-domain tokens matter, so filling the K-to-T gap with mostly-clean target-like docs (unlike experiment 3's off-domain filler) should beat repeating the core.
outcome: dev 1.9269 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Change only the dedup step so that it keeps the cleanest copy of each duplicate group instead of the first occurrence. Everything after it (pass 2 leave-one-out, worst-window rejection, 2-means, 0.5 T floor, T cap, seeded shuffle) stays unchanged.

1. Compute the head key (hash of the normalised first 500 chars) and the body key (hash of tokens 100..300, only if at least 50 tokens are there) for every doc, as now. Do not drop anything yet.
2. Build duplicate groups with union-find: two docs are in the same group if they share a head key or a body key.
3. Run pass 1 (target-only bigram model) on all docs with at least 50 tokens, duplicates included. Keep both outputs of _score_all: mean NLL and worst 256-token-window NLL.
4. In each group keep exactly one doc: the one with the lowest pass-1 worst-window NLL. Break ties by lower pass-1 mean NLL, then by larger full token count, then by lower index. Singleton groups are kept as they are.
5. The candidate set is these group representatives. Run the pass-1 2-means on the representatives' pass-1 scores only, then continue with pass 2 exactly as now.

Log the number of groups with more than one member, the number of groups where the chosen doc is not the first occurrence, and the final K/T (core tokens over T).
why: Keep-first dedup can keep a damaged copy (later rejected) and discard its clean twin, and experiment 4 suggests that losing clean in-domain tokens is costly, so choosing the cleanest copy per group should recover in-domain text without adding noise.
outcome: dev 1.9372 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Keep the core selection exactly as now (dedup, two-pass bigram, worst-window rejection, 2-means, 0.5 T floor, T cap). Change only how the T-token budget is filled when the core has K < T tokens: instead of letting the trainer cycle the shuffled list (which repeats an arbitrary prefix), build an explicit list of at least T tokens in which the repeated docs are the most target-like ones.

1. Keep the pass-1 scores (mean NLL under the target_sample-only bigram model) for all candidates; today only pass-2 scores are used after pass 1.
2. Compute the core as now. Let K be its total full token count. If K >= T, output is unchanged.
3. If K < T: rank the core docs by ascending pass-1 mean NLL (closest to the real target sample, not to the self-trained model). Walk down this ranking and add each doc as a second copy until the extra tokens reach T - K + 30,000 (a small overshoot so the trainer never wraps). If the ranking is exhausted first (K < 0.5 T), continue with third copies in the same order.
4. Concatenate the core and the extra copies and do one seeded shuffle of the whole list (CURATE_SEED), so the repeats are spread through training rather than clustered.
5. Log K/T, the number of docs repeated, the extra tokens, and the pass-1 NLL of the last repeated doc against the core median.
why: Adding filler, adding near-core docs and tightening the core all scored worse, so the composition of the core looks near its optimum and the untested lever is which docs get the T - K tokens of repetition; giving them to the docs closest to the real target sample should weight training towards the held-out distribution.
outcome: dev 1.9257 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, rejected

idea:
Replace the pool-geometry thresholds of pass 2 with thresholds calibrated on target_sample itself. Everything else (dedup, pass 1 with 2-means for the pseudo-target, leave-one-out pass 2, 0.5 T floor, T cap, seeded shuffle) stays unchanged.

1. Cap the target arrays at 2,000 tokens when fitting model2 (pass 1 still uses the full target arrays), so that leave-one-out on a target doc is exact.
2. After fitting model2 on capped target + pseudo-target docs, score the 200 capped target docs with model2 leave-one-out (in_fit = True for all of them) using the existing _score_chunk. This gives target mean NLLs `t_mean` and target worst-256-window NLLs `t_worst`. These show how real held-out target articles score under the model.
3. Mean-NLL threshold: thr_mean = percentile(t_mean, 97.5) + 0.05 nats. Keep candidates with scores2 <= thr_mean; this replaces the 2-means low-cluster mask.
4. Worst-window threshold: thr_worst = percentile(t_worst, 97.5) + 0.15 nats. Reject candidates with worst2 > thr_worst; this replaces `thr2 + 1.0`.
5. Safety: still compute the pass-2 2-means threshold thr2. If the calibrated selection has under 0.5 T tokens, the existing floor widens by best score as now. If thr_mean is not finite, fall back to thr2 and thr2 + 1.0.
6. Log thr2, thr_mean, thr_worst, the number of docs and tokens kept under the old and the new rule, and K/T.
why: The 2-means midpoint depends on where the junk happens to sit and may admit general web English or reject real articles, whereas leave-one-out scores of the 200 target docs show directly what in-domain text scores, so the cut-offs for both mean and worst-window NLL should be more accurate.
outcome: dev 1.8361 against 1.9172 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: Implement a weighted pass-2 score that favors higher quality content by increasing the influence of the worst-window NLL. Specifically, instead of a hard rejection on thr_worst, use a continuous penalty where scores2_weighted = scores2 + alpha * worst2, where alpha is set to 0.5. Then, apply the thr_mean threshold to this weighted score, while maintaining the thr_worst as a hard ceiling/cutoff.
why: Hard thresholds can be brittle; a weighted score penalizes docs with local 'glitches' while allowing very high-quality docs with minor imperfections to persist, potentially creating a smoother transition in the distribution of the training data.

idea: Implement a 'content-depth' filter by analyzing the entropy of the bigram transitions in each candidate. Specifically, for each document, calculate the variance of the NLL values across its 256-token windows. Reject documents where the variance is extremely high (indicating high structural incoherence) or where the mean NLL of the first 500 tokens is significantly higher than the mean NLL of the subsequent tokens (indicating a 'bait and switch' structure where a clean title is followed by junk/spam). Use the target_sample to define the expected NLL range and variance.
why: This addresses docs that might pass the mean NLL and worst-window checks but contain high-variance structural shifts or 'bait-and-switch' content that degrades the model's ability to learn coherent long-form distributions.
